Divided into 12 rolls: 1940 / 12 = 161.7 grams per piece at scaling. Sanity check: the percentages sum to 194, and 194 percent of 1000 grams is 1940, agreeing by the aggregate route. Two production notes. The scaling weight 161.7 is the dough-out-of-the-bowl figure; expect to lose a few grams to the bowl, the bench, and your hands, so production bakers scale pieces at 161.7 and accept the last piece running slightly light, or bump the batch by 1 percent and keep the piece weight honest. And the butter at 250 grams is a quarter of the flour weight, which is what makes this dough enriched and fragile: its percentage is the one to weigh most carefully, because butter weighed sloppily changes both richness and structure.

Two rooms get primed before different finish colors: room one has 417 square feet of wall, room two has 260. Primer covers 350 square feet per gallon. The finish paints are different colors and cannot be pooled, but the primer is shared. How much primer, and how does the pooling logic work?

Primer is one shared material, so its areas pool: 417 + 260 = 677 square feet. At 350 per gallon, 677 / 350 = 1.93, rounded up to 2 gallons. Those 2 gallons carry 700 square feet of coverage against 677 needed, leaving 23 square feet of coverage in hand for cutting in and touch-ups. Sanity check the pooling decision itself: had the primer been bought per room, each room would round up separately, 2 gallons for room one and 1 for room two, 3 total, so pooling saved a gallon. That saving exists because primer is fungible between the rooms in a way the finish colors are not; the finish paints must be figured room by room, each with its own ceiling step, exactly as in a takeoff table. The general rule decides every one of these questions: pool the areas only across surfaces that will genuinely draw from the same can, and round up at the level of the can, never higher and never lower.

Stair railing takeoff: 13 treads, riser 7.71 inches, tread run 10.5 inches. Balusters sit 3 per tread. How long is the rake of the handrail along the slope, how many balusters does the stair take, and how many should I order with spares?

The handrail follows the hypotenuse of one step, repeated 13 times. One step's slope length is the square root of 7.714 squared plus 10.5 squared, which is the square root of 169.7, about 13.03 inches. Over 13 treads the rake runs 169.4 inches, just over 14 feet, so the rail stock to buy is a 16 foot length, for the same angled-cut reasons as a stringer. Balusters: 13 treads x 3 per tread = 39. With spares for the inevitable split or miscut baluster, order 39 + 3 = 42. Sanity check the baluster spacing behind the count: 3 balusters per 10.5 inch tread puts them on roughly 3.5 inch centers, so the gaps between balusters stay under the 4 inch sphere rule that stair codes use to keep a child's head from passing through. The count and the code rule are the same fact viewed from two sides: if your per-tread count ever produces spacing over 4 inches, the count is wrong no matter how clean the multiplication looks, which is why railing takeoffs start from the spacing rule and derive the count, never the reverse.
Rich sugar syrup is 2:1 sugar to water by weight. I am making a batch starting with 500 grams of sugar. How much water, and what is the finished syrup weight before cooking loss?

A 2:1 ratio means two parts sugar to one part water, so the water is the sugar weight divided by 2: 500 / 2 = 250 grams. The batch before cooking is 500 + 250 = 750 grams. Sanity check: sugar is two thirds of 750, and two thirds is exactly what 2 parts of 3 means, so the split honors the ratio. Weighing syrup is the professional method because volume lies about sugar: a cup of granulated sugar weighs anywhere from 180 to 220 grams depending on crystal size and how it was scooped, a 20 percent swing that decides whether a cocktail or a sorbet sets properly. The ratio also tells you the syrup's strength directly: 2:1 is a 66.7 percent sugar solution, which is why rich syrup keeps for months refrigerated while 1:1, at 50 percent, molds in weeks. If you simmer the batch, a few percent of the water leaves as steam and the ratio creeps richer; syrups are therefore mixed by weight and heated only until the sugar dissolves, not boiled down.
Convert this baking formula from cups to grams using standard weights: flour 3.5 cups at 120 grams per cup, sugar 1.75 cups at 200, cocoa 0.5 cup at 85, butter 0.75 cup at 227. Table it with a total.

Each line is cups times that ingredient's own grams-per-cup; there is no universal cup weight, which is the entire point of the table:

| Ingredient | Cups | g per cup | Grams |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flour | 3.5 | 120 | 420 |
| Sugar | 1.75 | 200 | 350 |
| Cocoa | 0.5 | 85 | 42.5 |
| Butter | 0.75 | 227 | 170.25 |
| **Total** | | | **982.75** |

Sanity check the spread: a cup of sugar weighs two thirds more than a cup of flour and nearly two and a half times a cup of cocoa, so any conversion that used one flat figure for all four would be wrong on three lines out of four, by margins no oven forgives. The total 982.75 grams is the batch weight before baking and a useful production figure: portioning, costing, and scaling all run off it. Once a formula lives in grams it also becomes scalable by any factor with a single multiplication per line, and convertible to baker's percentages by dividing through by the flour, which is why professional formulas are born in grams and home recipes get converted exactly like this, once, and then kept.
Concrete at 1:2:4 (cement, sand, aggregate) using two 50 kilogram bags of cement. Give me sand, aggregate, and the mixing water at a water-cement ratio of 0.5 by weight.

Two bags fix the cement at 2 x 50 = 100 kilograms, and one part of the ratio is therefore 100 kilograms. Sand at 2 parts: 100 x 2 = 200 kilograms. Aggregate at 4 parts: 100 x 4 = 400 kilograms. Water at a water-cement ratio of 0.5: 100 x 0.5 = 50.0 liters, since a kilogram of water is a liter. Sanity check: the dry materials total 100 + 200 + 400 = 700 kilograms, seven times the cement, matching the ratio's seven parts. The water figure is the one with engineering weight on it: 0.5 is a sound structural ratio, and every extra 10 liters a mixer adds for easy shoveling raises it toward 0.6 and quietly taxes the finished strength by roughly a fifth. That is why the water is specified as a ratio to the cement and not as 'add until it looks right': the look of workable concrete is achievable across a wide band of ratios, but the strength is set by the number, and the number is set before the mixer starts turning.

Grout for two floors with the same grout: kitchen 45 square feet of 12x12 tiles, where a bag covers 100 square feet; bathroom 30 square feet of 6x6 tiles, where a bag covers only 55 square feet because smaller tiles mean more joints. How many bags total?

Grout consumption is driven by joint length, not floor area, which is why the two floors eat grout at different rates. Work in fractions of a bag: the kitchen uses 45 / 100 = 0.45 of a bag; the bathroom uses 30 / 55 = 0.545 of a bag. Because it is the same grout, the fractions pool: 0.45 + 0.545 = 0.995 of a bag in total, which rounds up to 1 bag. Sanity check: the pooled demand lands just under a whole bag, and buying per room would have meant 2 bags with nearly a full bag left over. The pooling works here for the same reason primer pooled across two rooms: one material, one can, fractions add. The caution is the near miss: 0.995 is close enough to 1.0 that a slightly larger bathroom or a wider joint pushes the job into a second bag mid-floor, and grout mixed from two bags can dry a shade different. When the pooled fraction lands above about 0.9, the second bag is cheap insurance against a color seam.
Deck footings: 8 concrete tube footings, each 12 inches in diameter and 36 inches deep. Bags of concrete mix yield 0.6 cubic feet each. How many bags?

A tube footing is a cylinder: pi times radius squared times depth. The radius is half the 12 inch diameter, 0.5 feet, and the depth is 3 feet, so one footing holds 3.14159 x 0.25 x 3 = 2.36 cubic feet. Eight footings: 18.85 cubic feet of concrete in total. At 0.6 cubic feet per bag, 18.85 / 0.6 = 31.4 bags, rounded up to 32 whole bags. Sanity check: 32 bags at 0.6 is 19.2 cubic feet against 18.85 needed, a margin of about a third of a bag per footing, which absorbs the bell at the bottom of each hole and the slight over-dig every auger produces. Cylinder volume is where footing estimates most often go wrong by a factor of two: using the diameter where the radius belongs quadruples the answer, since the radius is squared. If a footing count ever comes back at 120 bags for a deck, that is the error, and it is worth checking before the pallet is delivered and the return becomes your problem.
Painting a door, 36 by 80 inches, both sides plus edges, with a quart of trim paint that covers about 100 square feet. Is one quart enough for two coats?

One face of the door is 36 x 80 = 2,880 square inches, which is 20.0 square feet. Both faces: 20.0 x 2 = 40 square feet, and the edges add a little under 2 square feet more, call it 42 square feet per coat in round terms. Two coats double the coverage demand: about 80 square feet of coverage using the faces alone, roughly 84 with the edges. A quart covering 100 square feet therefore does the job with a small reserve, so yes, one quart is enough. Sanity check: a gallon covers about 400 square feet and paints roughly five doors two coats both sides by this arithmetic, which matches shop experience. The reserve matters because doors drink unevenly: end grain at the top and bottom edges, which should be sealed even though nobody sees them, takes paint like a sponge, and a door painted on a humid day may want a third pass on the flat panels. One quart, no second trip, but only just.
A soup recipe yields 2400 grams total and uses 1600 grams of stock. I need 15 portions of 220 grams each. What is the scale factor and how much stock?

Target yield first: 15 portions x 220 grams = 3300 grams of soup needed. The scale factor is target over original: 3300 / 2400 = 1.375. Stock scales by the same factor: 1600 x 1.375 = 2200 grams. Sanity check by proportion: stock was two thirds of the original yield (1600 of 2400), and 2200 is two thirds of 3300, so the structure of the soup is preserved, which is the definition of a correct scale. Yield-based scaling is how kitchens actually resize recipes, because portions are what is sold and served; the cook works backwards from covers to batch size to ingredients, exactly as here. Note the factor 1.375 is three significant figures of awkwardness that grams absorb without complaint. The same scale in cups would have produced a factor of 1.375 applied to quantities like 6.8 cups of stock, and the rounding errors would have started compounding before the pot was even on the stove.

Wallpaper strips: a wall is 12 feet wide and 8.5 feet high. The paper is 21 inches wide, rolls are 33 feet long, and each strip needs 9 feet of roll allowing for pattern trim. How many strips, how many strips per roll, and how many rolls?

Strips across the wall: the wall is 144 inches wide, each strip covers 21 inches, so 144 / 21 = 6.86, rounded up to 7 strips. Strips per roll: each strip consumes 9 feet of the 33 foot roll, and 33 / 9 = 3 whole strips with 6 feet left over, so 3 strips per roll; the floor function, not rounding, governs here because a partial strip is not a strip. Rolls needed: 7 / 3 = 2.33, rounded up to 3 rolls. Sanity check: 3 rolls yield 9 strips against 7 needed, leaving 2 strips of slack for a damaged drop or a misaligned pattern start, which on patterned paper is not generosity but necessity. Note the two different roundings in one problem: strips across and rolls round up (ceil), strips per roll rounds down (floor), because one counts things you must have enough of and the other counts things a fixed length can yield. Mixing those directions up is the most common takeoff error after the fencepost mistake.
I make a simple brine at 3 percent salt by weight of the water. For 1500 grams of water, how much salt? And what is the salt percentage of the finished brine, roughly?

Salt at 3 percent of the water weight: 1500 x 0.03 = 45 grams. The finished brine weighs 1500 + 45 = 1545 grams, so the salt as a percentage of the whole is 45 / 1545 x 100 = 2.91 percent. Sanity check: 2.91 is just under 3, and it must be, because the denominator grew by the salt itself; a percentage of the water and a percentage of the finished brine are different numbers describing the same bucket. This distinction is not pedantry: published brine charts come in both conventions, and a 3 percent-of-total brine made by the of-water method is slightly weaker than intended, while a strong curing brine at 10 percent made the wrong way is off by a full point, enough to matter for safety margins in cured meats. When a recipe just says 'percent brine' without the base, the tiebreaker is the source: American charcuterie usually means percent of water plus salt combined, home recipes usually mean percent of the water. Check the base before you weigh, because the salt cannot be un-dissolved.
Cutting plan: I need 6 pieces at 34 inches and 4 pieces at 47 inches, all cut from 8 foot (96 inch) boards of the same stock. How many pieces per board for each length, and how many boards total?

Pieces per board are a floor division, since a board yields only whole pieces:

| Piece length | Per 96 in board | Pieces needed | Boards |
|---|---|---|---|
| 34 in | 2 (68 in used, 28 in offcut) | 6 | 3 |
| 47 in | 2 (94 in used, 2 in offcut) | 4 | 2 |
| **Total** | | **10** | **5** |

Sanity check the totals: 5 boards bring 480 inches of stock for 6 x 34 + 4 x 47 = 392 inches of parts, leaving 88 inches of offcut, which the table accounts for as 3 x 28 + 2 x 2 = 88, balancing exactly. The two lengths waste very differently: the 47 inch pieces nearly tile the board, while the 34 inch pieces strand a 28 inch offcut per board. If those offcuts matched another part in the project, the plan would change completely, which is why cutting plans are optimized across the whole part list at once rather than length by length. Also uncounted here: the saw kerf, about an eighth of an inch per cut, which this plan absorbs inside its offcuts but which a tighter plan must subtract explicitly per cut.

Garden sprayer concentrate doses at 30 milliliters per liter of water. My sprayer holds 8 liters. How much concentrate per fill, and how many full sprayer fills do I get from a 500 milliliter bottle? What is left in the bottle?

Per fill: 30 x 8 = 240 milliliters of concentrate. Fills per bottle: 500 / 240 = 2.08, and fills are whole, so 2 full fills, using 2 x 240 = 480 milliliters. Left in the bottle: 500 - 480 = 20 milliliters. Sanity check: 20 milliliters is less than one fill's dose of 240, confirming no third fill is hiding in the bottle, and it is also less than a single liter's dose short by only 10 milliliters, which is why the leftover feels tantalizingly close to useful. Keep it rather than stretching it: topping up a third fill with 20 milliliters and extra water mixes that load at 25 milliliters per liter instead of 30, a sixth under strength, and pest and weed products have label rates that are legal limits in both directions, not suggestions. The floor division for fills and the ceiling division for purchases are the same rule seen from opposite ends: what a container yields rounds down, what a job requires rounds up.
Deck stain: deck is 16 by 12 feet, two coats, stain covers 200 square feet per gallon per coat on smooth decking. How many gallons?

Deck area: 16 x 12 = 192 square feet. Two coats need 192 x 2 = 384 square feet of coverage. At 200 per gallon, 384 / 200 = 1.92 gallons, rounded up to 2 gallons. Sanity check: 2 gallons deliver 400 square feet of coverage against 384 needed, a margin of 16 square feet, which is slim; one gallon would cover barely half the first coat's second pass. The slim margin deserves a comment: coverage figures assume smooth, sound decking, and weathered boards with raised grain drink noticeably more, particularly on the first coat, which is doing double duty as sealer. If the deck is grey and thirsty, the honest order is 2 gallons plus a quart, or accept that the second coat on the last boards gets rolled thin and shows it by midsummer. Stain, unlike paint, cannot be stretched by thinning without changing the color, because the pigment load is the product.
A pizza dough batch totals 1800 grams. Dough balls are scaled at 270 grams. How many balls, and what is left over?

Balls are a floor division: 1800 / 270 = 6.67, so 6 full balls, using 6 x 270 = 1620 grams. Leftover: 1800 - 1620 = 180 grams of dough. Sanity check: 180 is two thirds of a ball, not enough to stretch to a seventh full-weight ball, and dividing the batch seven ways instead would give 257 gram balls, uniformly under spec. Production kitchens treat the 180 gram remainder as a feature: it becomes the tester ball that gets baked first to check the oven, or a small focaccia for the crew, or it is folded into tomorrow's batch as old dough. What you do not do is distribute it silently across the six balls at 30 grams each; a 300 gram ball in a 270 gram system changes bake time and portion cost on every pizza. Scaling weights are a promise to the rest of the system, oven timing, box size, menu price, and the remainder is handled openly or not at all.

Painting 800 square feet of wall, two coats, but the walls have a heavy orange-peel texture that cuts coverage from 350 to 300 square feet per gallon. How many gallons, and what did the texture cost me versus smooth walls?

Two coats over 800 square feet is 1600 square feet of coverage demand. At the textured coverage of 300 per gallon: 1600 / 300 = 5.33 gallons, rounded up to 6 gallons. On smooth walls at 350, the same job is 1600 / 350 = 4.57, rounded up to 5 gallons. So the texture costs one full gallon on this job. Sanity check: the coverage penalty is 50 square feet per gallon, about 14 percent, and the true extra demand is 1600/300 - 1600/350 = 0.76 gallons, which the ceiling step rounds to a whole gallon because purchases are integers; the true cost is about three quarters of a gallon and the paid cost is one, the difference being the purchasable-unit rounding again. Texture drinks paint for a simple geometric reason: the actual surface area of an orange-peel wall is larger than its measured flat area, every bump presenting two slopes to the roller, and the valleys hold paint that contributes nothing to coverage. Heavy knockdown textures can cut coverage by a quarter; when the texture is severe, prime first, because primer is cheaper than finish paint and the first coat is the thirsty one.

Thinset coverage depends on trowel notch: a bag covers 95 square feet with a 3/16 inch notch, 65 with a 1/4 inch, and 40 with the 1/2 inch notch that large format tile requires. My floor is 120 square feet of large format. Bags needed at the correct notch, and what goes wrong if I buy for the 1/4 inch figure?

At the required 1/2 inch notch: 120 / 40 = 3 exactly, so 3 bags. At the 1/4 inch figure you would buy 120 / 65 = 1.85, rounded up to 2 bags. Those 2 bags spread at the big notch cover only 80 square feet of the 120 at proper depth, and the real failure is worse than running short: large format tile on a starved bed gets poor contact coverage, and the standard requires 95 percent contact in wet and exterior work, so tiles laid to stretch the mortar are hollow, fragile, and loud underfoot. Sanity check the coverage ladder itself: doubling the notch depth from 1/4 to 1/2 a bit more than halves the coverage, 65 down to 40, because the ridges are both taller and wider apart. The notch is not a suggestion about style; it is the metering device that sets mortar volume per square foot, exactly as a ratio sets oil per liter of fuel. Buy 3 bags, and let the trowel, not the budget, choose the notch.

Jam: 3.2 kilograms of fruit, sugar at a ratio of 0.75 kilograms per kilogram of fruit. Cooking loses 10 percent of the total mass. Jars hold 340 grams. How much sugar, what is the finished jam mass, and how many full jars?

Sugar: 3.2 x 0.75 = 2.4 kilograms. Total mass into the pot: 3.2 + 2.4 = 5.6 kilograms. After the 10 percent cooking loss, finished jam is 5.6 x 0.9 = 5.04 kilograms, which is 5040 grams. Full jars at 340 grams: 5040 / 340 = 14.8, so 14 full jars, with about 280 grams left over for the cook's toast and the refrigerator jar. Sanity check: 14 jars hold 4,760 grams, and the remainder of roughly 280 grams is less than a jar, consistent. The cooking loss is the step home preservers most often skip, and it cuts both ways: jars planned from raw mass come up short, as here by nearly a jar, and sugar concentration planned from raw mass comes out low, because the loss is almost entirely water, meaning the finished jam is sweeter and more concentrated than the pot suggested. Yield arithmetic for anything cooked, jam, soup, or stock, must run through the loss factor before it meets a jar count, a portion count, or a price.
Coffee brewing at a 1:16 ratio, coffee to water by weight. I am using 45 grams of coffee. How much water, and how many 240 gram mugs does that brew?

Water is 16 parts against the coffee's 1 part: 45 x 16 = 720 grams of water, which is 720 milliliters since water weighs a gram per milliliter. In mugs: 720 / 240 = 3.0 mugs of brew, before accounting for the water the grounds absorb. Sanity check: a 1:16 ratio is a 6.25 percent coffee concentration by weight, and 45 / (45 + 720) = 5.9 percent of the total brew mass, close to the ratio figure with the small difference being the coffee's own mass in the denominator, the same base subtlety as brine percentages. The absorption note is real: grounds hold roughly twice their weight in water, about 90 grams here, so the poured yield is closer to 630 grams, or two and a half honest mugs. Brew ratios are specified on water in, not coffee out, precisely because absorption varies with grind and method; if you plan mugs for guests, plan from yield, and if you plan strength, plan from the ratio, and do not confuse the two ledgers.
Blown attic insulation: one bag covers 55 square feet at the target depth for R-30. The attic is 900 square feet. How many bags, and why do I not just divide and buy the exact figure?

The division gives 900 / 55 = 16.36 bags, and bags are whole, so the purchase is 17 bags. Sanity check: 17 bags cover 935 square feet at target depth, a 35 square foot margin, while 16 bags would cover 880, leaving a 20 square foot strip of attic at low depth, and in insulation the thinnest strip sets the performance of the whole ceiling because heat flow concentrates where resistance is lowest. That asymmetry is why insulation is never bought to the exact figure even beyond the purchasable-unit rule: coverage on the bag assumes a uniform depth that no attic has, with eaves that taper, hatches, joist tops, and ductwork all stealing or thinning coverage. The extra bag is also the cheapest bag of the job, because rental machines for blowing insulation are typically free with a minimum bag purchase that this order clears anyway. Depth, not area, is the deliverable: mark depth rulers on the trusses before starting and blow to the ruler, because the bag count is an estimate and the ruler is a measurement.

Final takeoff table for a small bathroom remodel: floor 40 square feet tiled with 12x24 tiles at 10 percent waste; walls 260 square feet, two coats of paint at 350 square feet per gallon; thinset at the back-buttered coverage of 40 square feet per bag; grout at 90 square feet per bag. Every line item, please.

Each material figured on its own coverage logic, every purchasable unit rounded up on its own line:

| Item | Working | Buy |
|---|---|---|
| Floor tiles, 12x24 (2 sq ft each) | 40 x 1.1 / 2 = 22.0 | 22 tiles |
| Wall paint, 2 coats | 260 x 2 / 350 = 1.49 gal | 2 gal |
| Thinset, back-buttered coverage | 40 / 40 = 1.0 | 1 bags |
| Grout | 40 / 90 = 0.44 | 1 bag |

Sanity check the table as a system: the tile line lands exactly on a whole number, 22 tiles, because the 10 percent waste on 20 tiles of coverage is exactly 2 tiles; the paint line carries the only real rounding slack, about half a gallon, which is the cutting-in and touch-up reserve; thinset at exactly 1 bag has no slack at all and is the line a prudent buyer bumps by one, because running out of thinset mid-floor is a stop-work event while an unopened bag is returnable. That last judgment, knowing which exact figure to distrust, is the difference between a takeoff and a shopping list: the arithmetic is the floor of the order, and experience decides where to stand above it.
